metadata.title: Who Decides It's A Bug?
metadata.commissioned_topic: Implications/Advantages of using AI as a Beta Tester for games and other kinds of software
metadata.note: ai-explainer spine. THREE primary sources, each read directly: the OSS-Fuzz README (figures dated May 2025), the OSS-Fuzz-Gen README (30 reported bugs; grading metrics), and Macnamara-style verbatim extraction from Meta's TestGen-LLM paper (arXiv:2402.09171, FSE'24). FRAMEWORK: WHAT IS THE ORACLE / WHAT HAPPENS TO A FAILURE IT CANNOT JUDGE / WHO PAYS FOR A FALSE POSITIVE. The reel is organised as three oracle regimes: free (crash), writable (spec), absent (fun/balance). Hero is B05, the paper's own sentence that it cannot tell a real bug from a bad assertion and therefore DISCARDS failing tests. B07 carries three source problems including the abstract-vs-body 11.5% vs ~10% discrepancy and the shifting denominator. The Nov 2024 Google Security Blog figure of 26 is NOT used — the page body could not be extracted, so it stays off screen.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — composer, ask lands answered. Speaks the author's name.
beats.narration_text: I'm Uday Sonawane. Can an AI do beta testing for your game or your software? The honest answer splits in two, and the thing that splits it has a name in the literature. It is called the oracle problem.
beats.new_visual_element: Claude composer, the topic question answered

props.segment: Uday Sonawane · Who Decides It's A Bug?
output: where a crash is the test: enormous scale

beats.role_note: premise split — a beta tester does four jobs, and automation is wildly uneven across them
beats.narration_text: Start by splitting the job. A beta tester does four things. They exercise the software in ways nobody designed for. They notice that something is wrong. They judge whether it matters. And they write it down so somebody else can reproduce it. Those are four different jobs, and automation is not uniformly good at them. It is extraordinary at the first, and the whole argument lives in the second.
beats.new_visual_element: the four jobs, the second marked

shot.show: explore / notice something is wrong / judge whether it matters / report it reproducibly
shot.visual_intent: Four bordered chips stacked in a column, numbered. The second, 'notice that something is wrong', is terracotta and carries a small chip beside it reading 'this one has a name'. A line beneath: these are four jobs, not one.

beats.role_note: PROOF rubric — three questions, AS A STRUCTURE before any figure
beats.narration_text: Three questions, and you can ask them of any testing tool anyone tries to sell you. One: what is the oracle — what decides that the output is wrong, rather than merely surprising. Two: what happens to a failure the tool cannot judge — does it get escalated, or quietly dropped. Three: who pays for a false positive — because somebody always does, and it is usually an engineer's afternoon.
beats.new_visual_element: the three questions, as a numbered structure

shot.show: three numbered cards: WHAT IS THE ORACLE / WHAT HAPPENS TO A FAILURE IT CANNOT JUDGE / WHO PAYS FOR A FALSE POSITIVE
shot.visual_intent: Three bordered cards land in a row, one per narration step. The first lands in terracotta — it is the question the rest of the reel answers three different ways — and the reel is scored against all three.

beats.role_note: case 1 — the free oracle, and the scale it buys. Names the technique honestly.
beats.narration_text: Case one: the oracle is free. If the program crashes, nobody has to judge anything — the crash is the verdict. That is what fuzzing exploits: throw malformed input at software until it falls over. Google runs this continuously as a project called OSS-Fuzz, and its own repository states that, as of May twenty twenty-five, it has helped identify and fix over thirteen thousand vulnerabilities and fifty thousand bugs across a thousand projects. Note the wording, which is theirs: helped identify and fix. And note what this is not. Classical fuzzing is not AI. It is a loop with a free oracle.
beats.new_visual_element: the free oracle and its scale, with the technique named accurately

shot.show: crash = free oracle; OSS-Fuzz 13,000 vulnerabilities / 50,000 bugs / 1,000 projects, as of May 2025
shot.visual_intent: Left, a bordered card: 'the oracle' over 'did it crash?' with a tick. Right, stacked, three figure cards reading 13,000 vulnerabilities, 50,000 bugs, 1,000 projects, with 'as of May 2025' beneath. A terracotta chip spans below: 'classical fuzzing is not AI — it is a loop with a free oracle'. Citation strip names the repository.

beats.role_note: case 2 — where AI actually enters: it writes the target, not the verdict
beats.narration_text: Case two is where AI enters, and it enters in a specific place. Google's OSS-Fuzz-Gen uses language models to write the fuzz targets — the little harness programs that decide which corner of the code gets hammered. The model writes the probe. The crash still delivers the verdict. Its repository reports thirty new bugs or vulnerabilities found by automatically generated targets, and the framework grades those targets on whether they compile, whether they crash the program, and how much new code they reach. That is a real contribution. It is also a contribution to reach, not to judgement.
beats.new_visual_element: the LLM writes the probe, not the verdict

shot.show: LLM writes the target; the crash still decides; 30 reported bugs; graded on compile/crash/coverage
shot.visual_intent: A horizontal three-stage flow: 'LLM writes the fuzz target' in terracotta, arrow, 'the target runs' in ink, arrow, 'the crash decides' in ink with a tick. Beneath, a panel of the framework's own grading metrics: compilability, runtime crashes, coverage. A chip: 30 new bugs/vulnerabilities reported. Citation strip.

beats.role_note: HERO BEAT — the oracle problem stated by the people who shipped the tool
beats.narration_text: Case three: the oracle has to be written, and now it gets hard. Meta built a tool called TestGen-LLM that uses language models to improve existing unit tests, and they published it. Here is the sentence that matters, from the paper itself. Without an automatable test oracle, the tool cannot automatically determine whether a failing test has found a bug, or whether it merely contains an incorrect test assertion. Read that again with a beta tester in mind. A failing test is the entire point of testing. And because the tool cannot tell a real bug from a bad assertion, it discards the failures.
beats.new_visual_element: the quoted limitation, and what it implies

shot.show: the paper's own sentence, and the consequence: failing tests are discarded
shot.visual_intent: A large bordered quotation card carrying the sentence verbatim with attribution beneath. Below it, in terracotta, a short flow: 'test fails' arrow 'is it a bug, or a bad assertion?' arrow 'cannot tell' arrow 'discarded'. Citation strip names the paper.

beats.role_note: what it does deliver — a funnel that narrows at every step and ends at a person
beats.narration_text: So what does it deliver, when it is working. In Meta's offline evaluation on Instagram Reels and Stories, seventy-five percent of its generated tests built correctly. Fifty-seven percent passed reliably. Twenty-five percent increased coverage. Deployed across Instagram and Facebook, it improved about ten percent of the classes it was applied to — a hundred and ninety-six out of nineteen hundred and seventy-nine — and seventy-three percent of its suggestions were accepted by engineers. Look at the shape of that. It narrows at every step, and the last step is a human deciding.
beats.new_visual_element: the funnel, and who stands at the end of it

shot.show: 75% built / 57% passed / 25% increased coverage; 196 of 1,979 classes; 73% accepted
shot.visual_intent: Four descending bars, proportional, labelled 75% built, 57% passed reliably, 25% increased coverage, and beneath them a separate pair: 196 of 1,979 classes improved, and 73% accepted. The last element is a terracotta chip reading 'the final gate is a person'. Citation strip.

beats.role_note: three source problems I hit, including one that cuts the headline figure
beats.narration_text: Now the part where I check my own sources, and all three have problems. First: that Meta paper's abstract says the tool improved eleven and a half percent of classes. The body says about ten percent, and gives the count — a hundred and ninety-six of nineteen seventy-nine, which is nine point nine. The eleven and a half appears only in the abstract, with no count anywhere. I used ten. Second: the abstract reports those percentages as percentages of test cases, while the results section reports them as test classes with at least one new test case. Those are different claims. Third: the two official OSS-Fuzz pages disagree with each other — the README says thirteen thousand as of May twenty twenty-five, the documentation site says ten thousand as of August twenty twenty-three. I used the newer one and put the date on screen.

shot.show: 11.5% abstract vs ~10% body; test cases vs test classes; two official pages disagreeing
shot.visual_intent: Three stacked rows, each a terracotta panel: the abstract-versus-body figure with the arithmetic 196/1,979 = 9.9%; the shifting denominator, cases versus classes; and the two OSS-Fuzz pages with their different dates and numbers. Citation strip: every figure on screen carries its date.

beats.role_note: scored, then the specific answer for games, then both sides
beats.narration_text: Score it. What is the oracle: a crash, free, and it scales enormously. A specification, writable, and it works with a human at the end. Or nothing at all — and for games that is most of the question. Is this level fun. Is this difficulty curve cruel. Is this tutorial confusing. Nobody can write that predicate, so there is nothing to automate. So be excited that the crash-hunting half of beta testing is being industrialised, and that a model writing probes found bugs in code that had already been fuzzed hard. And be sceptical of anyone selling AI beta testing without telling you what their oracle is, because that answer determines everything else.
beats.new_visual_element: the rubric scored, then both sides

shot.show: three oracles scored; the games case; be excited / be sceptical
shot.visual_intent: Three ticked rows restating the rubric with its answer: crash, specification, nothing. The third row carries the games examples in soft ink. Beneath, two bordered cards side by side: BE EXCITED in ink, BE SCEPTICAL in terracotta, two short lines each. Citation strip.

beats.role_note: scaffolded task with a GOOD/BAD discriminator
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Take any testing tool you use or are being sold, and ask it one question: what decides that a result is wrong. Then ask what it does with a failure it cannot classify.
